newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan Q&A, PART VI - Budget amendment, credit.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan Q&A, PART VI - Budget amendment, credit.

text.p: The following are excerpts from the question and answer session following the first leg of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins address before Congress.
Greenspan addressed the Senate Banking Committee at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
SEN. FAIRCLOTH: "Do you think a Constitutional amendment to balance the budget would threaten Social Security?"

GREENSPAN: "I'm not in favor of a balanced budget amendent. I don't like economic policy to be embodied in a document such as the American Constitution, which is a set of principles rather than operational imperatives.
"Secondly, should the Congress and/or the administration fail to live up to the Constitutional amendment, then it falls to the courts, which can do numbers of different things.

"I see no reason why any particular program is at risk or any tax level or rates at risk any more than any others. What that would apparently do is put to the courts a solution to expenditure and receipts side, but there's nothing in that process which suggests to me that any particular element is any more at risk than any of the others."

SEN BENNETT: "I would like you to comment about the rise in credit card debt and the impact of people having access to credit that is the most seductive and at the same time the most expensive that a consumer can have.
"I'm not one who says we should make sure credit cards are not available to students and such, but the overall numbers are getting a little scary in terms of delinquencies and bankruptcies."
GREENSPAN: "You're certainly correct that deliquencies have been rising quite substantially. While there is no direct relationship, the sharp rise in personal bankruptcies is quite startling.

"Credit card debt has been profitable for those who issue it largely because, at the interest rates the markets seem to converge on, you can take some fairly substantial losses and still have some fairly good rates of return on capital.

"Nonetheless, there's been some pulling back on the part of lenders who have been startled by the fact that whereas in years past they could trace 30-day delinquencies, 60-day delinquencies, default at some point. Right now, they go from good risk to default with nothing in between. No warning signs.
"I think it's a particular localized problem. It is not a large number. It's a relatively small part of aggregate household debt and not a major factor in the economy.
"Because there is increasing awareness of the risks involved, my judgment is that the banking system is taking appropriate action and pulling back."
